Acrylic vs glass home elevator cab

Owners shop the $18,995 pneumatic home elevator installed special, then ask: “Can we do glass instead of the tube?” That sounds like a finish upgrade. It is a cab invoice and more set hours. The cheap special is an acrylic through-floor tube. Glass is a different ticket on the same house.

Open the free home elevator bid calculator

The tube is not a glass cab

On a typical two-stop through-floor cheap special — $52 wage, 32% burden, 15% overhead, 20% target margin, ten miles — acrylic bids $28,108.09 (walk-away $22,486.47). A standard enclosed cab adds $2,834.17. Wood-panel adds $5,044.01. Glass adds $8,354.52 and bids $36,462.61 (walk-away $29,170.09). Those add-ons are the cab kits. They do not change the drive or the shaft.

Matching the acrylic number loses the cab ticket

If they already shopped the tube and you send the acrylic $28,108.09 on a glass-cab ask, you sit $1,062.00 under the glass walk-away of $29,170.09. Matching the published $18,995 pneumatic dump on that glass job loses about $10,175. The same glass add-on ($8,354.52) shows up on a hydraulic shaft house — the cab ticket does not shrink because the shaft got more expensive.

Common questions

Is an acrylic vacuum-tube cab the same bid as a glass home elevator cab?

No. The cheap special is an acrylic through-floor tube. A glass cab is more hours and a cab invoice. On a typical two-stop pneumatic cheap special — $52 wage, 32% burden, 15% overhead, 20% target margin — acrylic bids about $28,108. Glass on the same house bids about $36,463, an $8,355 upgrade.

How much extra should I charge for a glass home elevator cab?

Using the calculator's starting cab kits, glass adds about $8,355 to the installed bid over acrylic on the same house. A standard enclosed cab adds about $2,834. Wood-panel adds about $5,044. Those add-ons are the cab ticket — they do not change the shaft or the drive.

What happens if I match the acrylic price on a glass-cab ask?

You eat the cab invoice and the extra set hours. Matching the $28,108 acrylic bid on a glass-cab cheap special sits about $1,062 under the glass walk-away of $29,170. Matching the published $18,995 pneumatic dump on that glass job loses about $10,175.

how-much-to-charge-to-install-a-home-ele.text:
← Home elevator bid calculator

How much to charge to install a home elevator

Accessibility and elevator contractors get shopped on a published $18,995 pneumatic home elevator installed Facebook special. Those numbers cannot see the shaft or the pit. Two stops of through-floor vacuum tube is a different job from a three-stop hydraulic in a new wood hoistway with a pit, a 240 V feeder, auto doors, battery lowering, and a state inspection.

Open the free home elevator bid calculator

Price the stops and the shaft, not the $18,995 dump

A home elevator is stops and travel, then a drive, then a hoistway. Pneumatic vacuum is a through-floor tube with no shaft. Winding drum is compact cable. Hydraulic is a ram, a pit, and a machine closet. Traction MRL is taller travel without a machine room. Through-floor is two deck cuts. A new wood shaft is framed. Masonry is CMU. Glass is a showpiece.

Pneumatic versus hydraulic on the same house

Homeowners usually start from the pneumatic special, then ask whether “a real elevator” is “a little more.” On the same stops it is not a little more. Hydraulic buys a unit, a pit, and a closet. A new shaft is a carpentry or masonry ticket of its own. The calculator prices all four drives on the house you already measured so you can quote the shaft job instead of matching the pneumatic number on a hydraulic install.

Through-floor is not a new wood shaft

The cheap special is almost always two stops of pneumatic through-floor, acrylic tube, no pit, no feeder, no permit. A three-stop hydraulic in new wood is a different crew week. Matching a published pneumatic number on a shaft job is how a sold install becomes a loss when the hoistway and the extras eat the margin.

This is not a stair lift, a ramp, or a walk-in tub

A stair lift is a chair on a rail — no shaft, no pit, no cab. A wheelchair ramp is carpentry: rise-to-run and landings. A walk-in tub is alcove plumbing. A walk-in shower is tile, slope, and glass. This prices a home elevator: stops, drive, hoistway, and extras.

Walk-away price

Load the wage with payroll burden. Add overhead as a share of direct cost. Then take margin as a share of the customer’s price, not a markup on cost. The walk-away number is total cost. A proposed price under that number loses money before you take anything out of it.

Hospital discharge is not the weekday bid

Families also shop a third special: “Mom comes home Friday — same $18,995 on Saturday?” A home elevator unit ships from the factory. Next-day air is a ticket on top of the rail-sized crate a stair-lift uses. Working around someone who just came home is a slower set. Saturday is overtime plus a weekend inspector. See should I expedite a home elevator for hospital discharge — on the cheap special that rush is about $7,812 over weekday, not a courtesy.

They asked for glass after shopping the tube? See acrylic vs glass home elevator cab — on the cheap special that upgrade is about $8,355, not a finish allowance. Customer already bought the unit? See should I install a customer-supplied home elevator — the $4,995 “just set what I bought” number is a different job from the $18,995 installed special.

This page is a walkthrough of the arithmetic in the home elevator bid calculator. It is not an elevator specification, a structural design, a building-code determination, an accessibility determination, or a price you should copy onto a contract.

Common questions

How much should I charge to install a home elevator?

Charge from stops, travel feet, drive, hoistway, and extras — not a published $18,995 pneumatic special. A two-stop through-floor vacuum tube is a different job from a three-stop hydraulic in a new wood shaft with a pit, a 240 V feeder, auto doors, battery lowering, and a state inspection.

Is a pneumatic vacuum elevator the same bid as a hydraulic shaft elevator?

No. Pneumatic vacuum is a through-floor tube with no shaft and no pit. Hydraulic needs a pit and a machine closet. Traction MRL is taller travel without a machine room. Matching a pneumatic special on a hydraulic-plus-shaft job is how a sold install becomes a loss when the hoistway and the extras eat the margin.

How do a new shaft, a pit, and a 240 V feeder change a home elevator price?

Through-floor is a pair of deck cuts. A new wood shaft is framed. Masonry is CMU. Glass is a showpiece. Price all five hoistways on the same house to see the upgrade. A pit, a machine closet, auto doors, battery lowering, a dedicated feeder, and a permit do not live in a published pneumatic dump.

Is this the same as a stair lift, a wheelchair ramp, or a walk-in tub?

No. A stair lift is a chair on a rail — no shaft, no pit, no cab. A wheelchair ramp is carpentry: rise-to-run and landings. A walk-in tub is alcove plumbing. This prices a home elevator: stops, drive, hoistway, and extras.

Should I install a customer-supplied home elevator?

Owners call with a crate in the garage: “I already bought a Stiltz / Savaria. Can you just install it for $4,995?” That sounds like free margin because the unit invoice left the bid. Open the free home elevator bid calculator

Zeroing the unit is not a free install

A contractor-supplied pneumatic tube still carries the unit invoice. An owner-supplied unit that actually fits zeros that line and keeps the same set hours. On a typical two-stop through-floor cheap special — $52 wage, 32% burden, 15% overhead, 20% target margin, ten miles — the contractor-supplied bid is about $28,108. Zeroing a $14,500 vacuum unit drops it to about $7,264, and the owner-supplied walk-away is about $5,811. Taking the Facebook special to “just set what they bought” at $4,995 still loses about $816. A $6,995 number keeps about $1,184 when the opening matches. A wrong opening still loses about $2,231.

vs-a-flat-pneumatic-special.html.text:
← Home Elevator Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat pneumatic special

"$18,995 pneumatic installed" is not a price for a job — it is a price for a through-floor tube with no shaft, quietly reused for every house that also asks for a home elevator.

What a flat pneumatic special is

A flat pneumatic special is the fastest way to quote a home elevator over the phone: quote the published tube number, skip the walkthrough. Homeowners shop it because a search result or a showroom flyer already gave them a figure, and it is the figure they will ask you to match — even for a job the tube was never priced on.

The number behind it was set for one kind of job — a two-stop through-floor cut with no shaft, no pit, and the lightest acrylic cab — and then reused for every house afterward, whether or not the next one needs a new hoistway, a pit, a 240 V feeder, or a heavier cab.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the stops, the travel feet, the capacity, the drive (pneumatic, winding drum, hydraulic, or traction MRL), the hoistway (through-floor, existing shaft, new wood, new masonry, or glass), the cab, and whether the job needs a pit, a machine closet, auto doors, battery lowering, a 240 V feeder, or a permit, plus your own wage, payroll burden, overhead, and target margin. It returns the bid price, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — for this drive and this hoistway, not a flat number for every house.

What a flat pneumatic special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same figure for a through-floor tube and a new-hoistway shaft job — even though framing a shaft alone can add days of labor and thousands in lumber and finish. Prices the hoistway per travel foot and per stop, separately for through-floor, existing-shaft reuse, new wood, new masonry, and glass.
Has no line for a pit, a machine closet, a 240 V feeder, auto doors, or battery lowering, regardless of whether the drive the customer wants actually needs them. Prices each of those as its own labor and material line, applied only when the job calls for it.
Quotes the same cab for an acrylic tube and a glass showpiece cab, with no separate line for finish. Prices acrylic, standard, wood-panel, and glass cabs as their own labor and material lines.
Has no separate line for a state elevator inspection, which a new-shaft job usually requires and a through-floor tube often does not. Prices the permit and inspection line separately, applied only when the job calls for it.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against what a flat pneumatic special would have quoted the same job, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two houses, one flat special

Using this calculator's own shipped presets, at a $52 hourly wage, 32% payroll burden, 15% overhead, and a 20% target margin:

The cheap-special preset — a two-stop pneumatic vacuum tube, through-floor cut, acrylic cab, 12 feet of travel, no shaft, no pit, no feeder — prices at $27,504.34, on a job that costs $22,003.47 to run.

Take the same house to a three-stop hydraulic in a new wood hoistway instead — wood-panel cab, 28 feet of travel, with a pit, a machine closet, auto doors, battery lowering, a 240 V feeder, and a permit — and the job costs $69,062.21 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator bids it at $86,327.77. Quoting the shaft job at the cheap special's own $27,504.34 price prices it $41,557.87 below its own break-even cost — before counting the $58,823.42 it falls short of this calculator's own bid price at the same 20% target margin. Same acrylic-tube special, one house that pays and one that loses money the moment the shaft is framed.

Common questions

Why does a flat pneumatic special get a home elevator install wrong?

Because the cost driver is the shaft and the extras, not the cab. A two-stop pneumatic vacuum tube cut through two floors needs no shaft, no pit, and no machine closet. A three-stop hydraulic in a new wood hoistway needs a framed shaft, a pit, a machine closet, a 240 V feeder, auto doors, battery lowering, and a state inspection, on top of a larger unit and more travel. A flat special charges both the same because it was priced on the cheapest drive and hoistway combination, not the job in front of the estimator.

What does a flat pneumatic special usually leave out entirely?

The shaft, the pit, the machine closet, the feeder, the auto doors, the battery lowering, and the permit. A published pneumatic number is set on a through-floor cut with an acrylic tube and no shaft -- it has no line for framing a new wood or masonry hoistway, no line for a pit or a machine closet a hydraulic or traction unit needs, no line for a 240 V feeder, and no line for the inspection a shaft job requires.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped presets, at a $52 hourly wage, 32% payroll burden, 15% overhead, and a 20% target margin: the cheap-special preset -- a two-stop pneumatic tube, through-floor, acrylic cab, 12 feet of travel -- bids at $27,504.34 on a $22,003.47 break-even cost. The losing-job preset -- a three-stop hydraulic in a new wood hoistway, wood-panel cab, 28 feet of travel, with a pit, a feeder, and a permit -- costs $69,062.21 to run before a dollar of profit. Quoting the shaft job at the cheap special's own $27,504.34 bid price prices it $41,557.87 below its own break-even cost, before counting the $58,823.42 it falls short of this calculator's own bid price at the same 20% target margin.

Is a flat pneumatic special ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of similar jobs -- a low-rise through-floor cut with no shaft, no pit, and a light acrylic or standard cab -- a flat special can land close, because that is probably the job the special was set on. The risk is quoting a new-shaft hydraulic or traction job the same way sight unseen, because the special does not know the drive, the hoistway, the cab, or which extras apply until someone walks the house, and by then the flat number has often already been quoted.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or material costs?

No. It has no data on your local labor market, your unit supplier's invoice pricing, or your permit fees. It takes the stops, the travel feet, the drive, the hoistway, the cab, and which extras apply, plus your own wage, burden, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat pneumatic special skips, not a market survey.
